newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan reels from China jitters, hog crisis.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan reels from China jitters, hog crisis.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday reeled from double blows to its economy as fears of new friction with rival China compounded what was shaping up as staggering damage from a crisis on the island's hog farms.
An unconfirmed Taiwan newspaper report that Beijing was planning April war games in three provinces near Taiwan sent the benchmark stock index plunging 3.49 percent.
The United Daily News quoted military intelligence as saying China planned the manoeuvres in a possible protest over a visit to Taiwan by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama.
Chinese provincial authorities cast doubt on the war games report, but the Taiwan dollar nonetheless took its biggest beating in months, losing T$0.08 against the U.S. dollar to close at T$27.625.

Experts said the China worries were exacerbating a far more fundamental crisis that has shaken Taiwan since Friday -- an outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease that promised thousands of layoffs and a slowing of economic growth.

"The pork disease has put Taiwan's entire economic recovery in jeopardy," said Grand Cathay Securities vice president Terry Chen. "Not only are pork exports completely shut down, the effect extends to related sectors like the feed industry."
Authorities determined to eradicate the scourge ordered the slaughter of all hogs -- even healthy ones -- at farms stricken with the fatal disease, meaning that about 100,000 animals will be killed.

Taiwan television showed graphic footage of masked soldiers in white plastic protective suits wielding electric prods to stun pigs, then using bulldozers and back-hoes to dump the animals -- many still alive -- into giant pits.

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong gave dramatic evidence of the magnitude of the pork crisis, saying an emergency ban on pork exports -- a multibillion-dollar farm sector -- could slash 0.5 percentage points from Taiwan's 1997 economic growth.
That would effectively erase a hard-won acceleration that since late 1996 appeared to have pushed Taiwan's gross domestic product growth back above six percent from 5.71 percent in 1996.
The news on the job front was equally grim, with authorities predicting up to 100,000 layoffs and a rise in 1997 joblessness to three percent -- well above a state forecast of 2.6 percent.
"In order for Taiwan's overall economy to maintain normal growth, other sectors like electronics would have to outperform expectations," said Chen of Grand Cathay.
Securities analysts predicted the stock market would enter a long profit-taking descent that could erase dramatic gains attained in 1997.

"Many investors worry that the disease will have a sharp impact on the overall economy," said United Securities analyst Lin Long-hsien. "They will be watching closely to see what kind of stabilising measures the government launches."
Central banker Sheu vowed to react appropriately in the face of any market-shaking contingency, adjusting liquidity levels as necessary in accordance with economic conditions.

"Please believe that the government has the power to deal with any fluctuations," Sheu told reporters when asked about the day's big market-moving factors. "The central bank will react appropriately, and when necessary will inject funds."
